'''Martha L. "Marty" Crump''' is a behavioral ecologist in the Department of Biology and the Ecology Center at [[Utah State University]] who studies [[amphibians]] and [[reptiles]].  Crump was the first individual to perform a long-term ecological study on a community of [[tropical]] amphibians, and did pioneering work in the classification of variability in [[amphibian]] [[Egg (biology)|egg]] size as a function of [[habitat]] predictability. She has co-authoried one of the most popular modern [[herpetology]] textbooks, ''Herpetology'' (1997–2015) as well as the memoir ''In Search of the Golden Frog'' (2000) and a number of other books for both adults and children.

==Childhood==
Martha L. "Marty" Crump was born in [[Madison, Wisconsin]], and her interest in [[ecology]] and the environment were spurred by her childhood spent in the [[Adirondack Mountains]] of upstate [[New York (state)|New York]].<ref name="Gold"/>

==Education and Research==
While an undergraduate at the [[University of Kansas]], she worked in the herpetology division of the Museum of Natural History, and after graduation, she participated in a faunal survey of [[amphibians]] and [[reptiles]] in a remote area of the upper Amazon Basin, [[Ecuador]]. She received her master's degree at the University of Kansas for her research in [[Brazil]] concerning amphibians and reptiles, and did her doctorate research in Ecuador on frogs’ reproductive behavior. After receiving her Ph.D. from the University of Kansas, she became a professor of zoology at the [[University of Florida]], where she continued her research in Ecuador, and also performed research in [[Costa Rica]] and [[Argentina]], focusing on amphibian parental care, [[cannibalism]], and [[reproduction]].<ref name="Gold">{{cite web|last=Gold|first=Donna|title=Popular Biologist Marty Crump Comes to COA|url=http://newsworthy.coa.edu/2012/02/marty-crump-comes-to-coa/|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130909174004/http://newsworthy.coa.edu/2012/02/marty-crump-comes-to-coa/|archive-date=September 9, 2013|access-date=8 September 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Crump was the first individual to perform a long-term ecological study on a community of [[tropical]] amphibians. She studied reproductive strategies in the [[neotropical]] [[anuran]] community at Santa Cecilia, Ecuador and recognized ten different modes of reproduction.<ref name="Hodl">{{cite journal|last=Hodl|first=Walter|title=Reproductive diversity in Amazonian lowland frogs|journal=Fortschritte der Zoologie|year=1990|volume=38|pages=41|url=http://homepage.univie.ac.at/Walter.Hoedl/Fortschr%20Zoologie%20Reproductive%20diversity.pdf|access-date=8 September 2013}}</ref> These categories were later modified and adapted for all anuran reproductive patterns that scientists are currently aware of.<ref name="Kaplan"/>

Crump was also a pioneer in classifying variability in [[amphibian]] [[Egg (biology)|egg]] size as a function of [[habitat]] predictability. Her research, focusing on tropical tree frogs, shows that in species that breed in temporary [[ponds]], individual females produce clutches that have a greater range of egg sizes while those breeding in permanent ponds have a very concentrated distribution, rarely deviating from the mean.<ref name="Kaplan">{{cite journal|last=Kaplan|first=Robert|author2=William S. Cooper|title=The Evolution of Developmental Plasticity in Reproductive Characteristics: An Application of The "Adaptive Coin-Flipping" Principle|journal=American Naturalist|date=March 1984|volume=123|issue=3|page=393|jstor=2461103|doi=10.1086/284211|s2cid=84632326}}</ref>

She has also been involved in several [[Conservation biology|conservation]] activities, including acting as a board member of the International Union for the Conservation of Nature as part of the DAPTF (Declining Amphibian Populations Task Force) from 2000 to 2010. She has held several editorial positions including Associate Editor of ''Herpetological Natural History'' from 2000 to 2006 and has served as an officer in several professional organizations including the American Society of Ichthyologists and Herpetologists, Society for the Study of Amphibians and Reptiles, and The Herpetologists’ League. She is currently the Program Officer for the annual scientific conference Joint Meeting of Ichthyologists and Herpetologists (JMIH).<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Crump|first1=Martha|title=JMIH Abstract Submission and Aftermath: The Process Demystified|journal=Herpetological Review|date=2017|volume=48|issue=4|pages=801–804|url=https://cpb-us-east-1-juc1ugur1qwqqqo4.stackpathdns.com/conferences.k-state.edu/dist/1/33/files/2018/01/JMIH-abstract-submission-2abdswy.pdf}}</ref>

Crump co-authored all four editions of one of the two most popular modern herpetology textbooks, ''Herpetology'' (1997–2015).  Her other books include a memoir, ''In Search of the Golden Frog'' (2000).<ref name="Donnelly"/>  In addition to books for adults, she has written several books for children, including ''Amphibians and Reptiles: An Introduction to Their Natural History and Conservation'' (2011) and ''The Mystery of Darwin's Frog'' (2013).<ref name="Bush"/><ref name="Kirkus"/>

In 1997, she received the Distinguished Herpetologist Award from The Herpetologists’ League. She has also received the American Society of Ichthyologists and Herpetologists [[Henry S. Fitch]] Award for Excellence in Herpetology (2020)<ref>{{cite web |title=Henry S. Fitch Award for Excellence in Herpetology |url=https://www.asih.org/awards/fitch-award |website=American Society of Ichthyologists and Herpetologists |publisher=American Society of Ichthyologists and Herpetologists |access-date=20 March 2026}}</ref> and the Society for the Study of Amphibians and Reptiles (SSAR) Presidential Award for Lifetime Achievement in Herpetology (2023).<ref>{{cite web |title=SSAR Presidential Award for Lifetime Achievement in Herpetology |url=https://ssarherps.org/ssar-awards/presidential-award/ |website=Society for the Study of Amphibians and Reptiles |publisher=Society for the Study of Amphibians and Reptiles |access-date=20 March 2026}}</ref>
